StringWithMarkup.String: 1,6-Hexanediol diacrylate (HDODA; CASRN 13048-33-4) was applied at a rate of 0 or 300 mg/kg once daily to the clipped backs of New Zealand White rabbits (5/sex/group) for 5 days/week for 2 weeks (10 treatments). The skin of 3 animals/sex/group was abraded. The treatment sites were left uncovered. Fifteen days after the initial treatment, 3 abraded-skin rabbits and 3 non-abraded rabbits (regardless of sex) were sacrificed. Two weeks following the last treatment, the remaining animals were sacrificed. One mortality in the treated group occurred on day 21; the cause was not determined. Treated animals exhibited erythema and edema at the application site after one dose. By the end of the second week, all treated animals showed severe erythema, slight to moderate edema, fissuring of the skin, desquamation, and eschar formation. Of the treated animals, 3 experienced slight weight loss, and several exhibited nasal discharge and loss of motor activity; these symptoms were attributed to causes other than treatment. At the interim sacrifice, microscopic examination of the skin revealed moderate irritation. At terminal sacrifice, skin sections showed intact epithelium but moderate to severe irritation. Microscopic examination of selected tissues revealed no evidence of systemic toxicity resulting from treatment with 300 mg/kg HDODA.

Inseminated female rats (6/group) were given 100, 500, or 1000 mg/kg C-255 in corn oil/day by oral gavage on days 6-15 of gestation. A control group received corn oil only.
